passage: On the wall above Suraj's bed in the Dharwad hostel hung a sheet of chart paper with thirty boxes. Every morning he coloured one in: green if he had slept by eleven and studied two hours, red if not. In the first week there were three reds. Harsha, his roommate, laughed at it. "Like a school kid's star chart." Suraj shrugged and kept colouring. By the third week, the greens ran in a line. He wasn't yawning in the morning lecture. The accounts problems that used to take him an hour now took twenty minutes. When the mid-term marks went up on the notice board, he stood in front of his name for a long time. Back in the room he looked at the chart, the long line of green. "I did that," he said quietly, and he felt taller. Harsha didn't laugh this time.

qa.q: What colour did Suraj use for a day he slept by eleven and studied two hours?
qa.a: Green.

qa.q: How did Suraj feel looking at the chart after the mid-term marks?
qa.a: He felt proud and taller, confident that the improvement came from his own steady choices.

qa.q: What made the chart useful rather than just a 'star chart'?
qa.a: It made his progress visible every day, so he could see the link between his actions and the better marks.

qa.q: How does Harsha's reaction change over the weeks?
qa.a: At first Harsha mocks the chart, but later stays quiet, seeming impressed by the results.

grounding: It shows a student who decides to fix his sleep and study schedule, records it, and gains confidence from seeing that he shaped the outcome.

passage: Yuki had failed two quizzes in her first term at university in Osaka. She blamed the early lectures and the long train ride. In the spring she tried something different. She bought a small notebook and wrote, each night, when she went to bed and how many hours she had studied. Bed by midnight. Two hours of reading before dinner. Some days she missed, and she wrote that too. Her friend Sami, from Finland, saw her writing on the train one morning. "Diary?" "Sort of. It's me keeping score." After six weeks, she flipped back through the pages. The midnight bedtimes stretched across whole weeks. And the quiz that morning had come back with a high mark. She sat still in the train, the notebook open on her knees, feeling something she hadn't felt all year: that she was steering.

qa.q: What did Yuki write in the notebook each night?
qa.a: When she went to bed and how many hours she had studied.

qa.q: What was Yuki feeling as she sat on the train with the notebook open?
qa.a: She felt proud and quietly confident, sure that she was steering her own life, after seeing the link between her record and her quiz mark.

qa.q: Why did writing down the missed days too help Yuki?
qa.a: Honest records showed the real pattern, so her improvement felt earned rather than lucky.

qa.q: How might Sami see Yuki's notebook habit?
qa.a: Sami might see it as a curious diary at first, and later as a clever way she took charge of her term.

grounding: It shows a student who fixes sleep and study schedules, records her progress, and gains confidence from seeing she authored the result.

passage: Last winter in Gangtok, my parents fought almost every night. About the shop, about my uncle, about everything. I lay in bed listening and made a list in my head of what I'd done wrong that day. Came home late. Got a C in chemistry. Forgot to buy milk. I was sure if I were better, they'd stop. So I tried to be perfect. I did the dishes before anyone asked. I studied till midnight. And still they fought. That made it worse; I thought I wasn't trying hard enough. It was Sangeeta aunty, our neighbour, who found me crying on the stairs one evening. I told her. She sat with me and said, "Pema, beti, grown-ups' fights are grown-ups' business. It is not your fault." She walked me home and spoke to my mother that night. I didn't believe her fully then. I'm starting to.

qa.a: What Pema had done wrong that day, like coming home late, getting a C in chemistry, and forgetting to buy milk.

Wednesday night

Shreya got caught copying in the physics test today. Madam took her paper and sent her to the principal. Shreya cried in the corridor, and all I could think was: it's my fault.

I lent her my notes on Monday. She said she'd study from them. If I'd made her study with me, she wouldn't have needed to copy. If I'd sat next to her. If I'd noticed she was stressed. I kept going round and round in my head.

At dinner Mumma asked why I wasn't eating. I told her. She said, "Mehak, you lent notes to help. Shreya chose what she did." I said yes, but I still feel sick.

Maybe she's right. It feels like I should have been able to stop it. Shreya won't answer my messages.

Going to sleep. Or trying.

— Mehak

passage: At the Saturday maths club in the community centre, Tarun sir always introduced Pooja the same way: "Our little genius." Pooja, eleven, smiled every time. This week he put up a hard olympiad problem and said, "Pooja, you'll crack this in two minutes." Everyone turned to look. Pooja stared at the board. She didn't know where to start. Her hands went cold. "I have a headache," she said, and asked to sit out. Later, when another girl solved it after several wrong tries, the class clapped. Pooja clenched her pencil hard enough to snap the lead. On the bus home, she told her mother she didn't want to go to maths club anymore. "It's too easy," she said, looking out of the window.

qa.q: What did Tarun sir call Pooja?
qa.a: Our little genius.

qa.q: Why did Pooja say she had a headache?
qa.a: She felt scared of failing in front of everyone after being called a genius, so sitting out felt safer than trying and getting it wrong.

qa.q: How could Tarun sir change his praise to help Pooja?
qa.a: He could praise the effort and different methods students try, so Pooja sees wrong tries as part of learning.

qa.q: How might the girl who solved the problem see Pooja's reaction?
qa.a: She might not notice or might think Pooja is upset with her, without knowing Pooja fears losing her label.

grounding: It shows a child repeatedly called a genius who avoids a hard problem to protect the label, feeling angry and pulling away.

passage: In Class 6 there was a word problem about trains that I could not do. I tried adding. Wrong. I tried drawing the trains on paper. Still wrong. Then I made a table with the times. That worked. When Jasleen ma'am checked it, she didn't say, "You're so smart." She said, "Yusuf, you tried three different ways, and the table worked. That's how you get better." I remember my ears going warm. After that, when a problem was hard, I didn't feel scared. I thought, okay, what's another way? I even started picking the starred questions at the end of each chapter, the hard ones, just to try. I'm in Class 8 now. I still make tables.

qa.q: What did Yusuf try first on the train problem?
qa.a: Adding.

qa.q: How did Yusuf feel when Jasleen ma'am praised the three methods?
qa.a: Yusuf felt proud and warm, and later less scared of hard problems, because the praise was about trying different ways.

qa.q: Why did Jasleen ma'am's praise help more than 'You're so smart'?
qa.a: It pointed to what Yusuf did, the methods and effort, so Yusuf learned that ability grows with trying, and started choosing hard questions.

qa.q: How might Jasleen ma'am feel seeing Yusuf pick the starred questions?
qa.a: She might feel pleased and encouraged, seeing that her specific praise helped Yusuf seek challenges.

grounding: It shows a teacher praising a child's different methods, which teaches that ability grows with effort and supports seeking challenges.

passage:
Class 5 note, Wednesday

Sachin has been stuck on long division for weeks. Today I watched him try one sum three ways: first repeated subtraction, then drawing groups, then the standard method with a small grid. The third way worked. Instead of saying "good boy" or "you're clever," I told him exactly what I saw: "You kept trying new methods when the first ones didn't work, and that's why you got it."

He looked surprised, then pleased. In the afternoon, when I offered an easy sheet or a harder one, he picked the harder one for the first time. He got two wrong and just said, "I'll try the grid."

I will keep noting what he does, not what he is.

— Reena

qa.q: How many methods did Sachin try on the sum?
qa.a: Three: repeated subtraction, drawing groups, and the standard method with a small grid.

qa.q: What did Sachin's choice of the harder sheet suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: It suggests he felt more confident and less afraid of mistakes after being praised for trying different methods.

qa.q: Why is Reena's praise more helpful than 'you're clever'?
qa.a: It names the specific effort and strategies Sachin used, showing him that trying new ways leads to success.

qa.q: How might Sachin see his own mistakes now?
qa.a: He seems to see them as a reason to try another method, like the grid, rather than as a sign that he's not clever.

grounding: It shows, through a teacher's note, how specific praise for a child's changing methods helps him believe ability grows and seek harder work.

passage:
Dear Diary,

Today in art, I was painting a tree and the leaves looked like green blobs. I tried a thin brush. Worse. I tried dabbing with a sponge. Better. Then I tried a toothbrush flick, like Seema ma'am showed last month. Leaves!

Seema ma'am came round and said, "Darshan, you didn't give up. You tried three tools and found what works. That's how painters get better." I felt happy all afternoon 😊

She didn't say I'm good at painting. She said I tried. And I think that's better, because I can always try, even if I'm not good yet.

Tomorrow I'm going to try a sky with the sponge. Skies are hard. But that's okay.

Darshan

qa.q: Which tool gave Darshan leaves that looked right?
qa.a: The toothbrush flick.

qa.q: How did Darshan feel after Seema ma'am's words?
qa.a: Darshan felt happy all afternoon and more confident to try harder things, like skies.

qa.q: What made Seema ma'am's praise useful for Darshan?
qa.a: It pointed out the effort and the tools tried, so Darshan learned that trying can always help, even without being good yet.

qa.q: How might Seema ma'am feel reading that Darshan wants to try a hard sky?
qa.a: Seema ma'am would likely feel proud that her specific praise helped Darshan seek a new challenge.

grounding: It shows a teacher praising a child's changing strategies, which teaches that ability grows with effort and encourages challenge seeking.

passage:
Tuesday

Art period again. We had to draw a still life: a jug, two onions, a cloth. Mine looked like a potato next to a lamp post. Tanvir's looked like a photo. Everyone crowded round his.

I erased mine three times, and then I just stopped. I wrote "not creative" at the bottom in tiny letters and closed the book.

Some people are born with it. Tanvir draws on every notebook margin and has since Class 3. Me, I'm a numbers person. It's fine. That's just how brains work.

Sir said it takes practice. Easy for him to say, he's an artist.

I'm dropping the art elective next term. No point wasting time on something I can't do.

— Farhan

qa.q: What did Farhan write at the bottom of the drawing?
qa.a: "not creative"

qa.q: Why does dropping the art elective feel sensible to Farhan?
qa.a: Farhan feels embarrassed and discouraged comparing the drawing to Tanvir's, and believes talent is fixed, so continuing seems pointless.

qa.q: What could Farhan try before deciding to drop art?
qa.a: Farhan could practise one small thing, like sketching the jug daily for two weeks, and compare the first and last drawings.

qa.q: How might Tanvir see Farhan's view that some people are born with it?
qa.a: Tanvir might feel it ignores all the years of margin doodles and practice behind his drawings.

grounding: It shows a teenager who is weak at drawing and decides they are just not creative, turning a current level into a permanent limit.

passage: The art room of the government girls' school in Sagar had one fan and thirty easels. Hemant sir asked the Class 9 students to draw the banyan tree outside the window. Sunaina tried. The trunk was too thin; the branches looked like sticks. The girl next to her had drawn every hanging root. Sunaina put down her pencil. "I'm just not creative, sir. Some people are born with it." Hemant sir said, "Your first try is where you start, not where you finish." She nodded politely, but after that, in every art class, she sat at the back doing her maths homework. When the annual exhibition came, Sunaina's section on the wall was empty. She walked past it quickly, telling herself it didn't matter.

qa.q: What did Hemant sir ask the students to draw?
qa.a: The banyan tree outside the window.

qa.q: Why did Sunaina walk past the empty section quickly?
qa.a: She felt a bit embarrassed and hurt, though she told herself it didn't matter, because believing she wasn't creative had stopped her from trying.

qa.q: What might help Sunaina keep trying at art?
qa.a: Starting with small, regular sketches of the tree and comparing them over weeks, as Hemant sir suggested, could show her that skill grows.

qa.q: How might Hemant sir see Sunaina's move to the back of the class?
qa.a: Hemant sir might feel disappointed and concerned, seeing her give up after one try.

grounding: It shows a teenager who is weak at drawing and says she's not creative, turning her current level into a permanent limit.

passage: At the music school in Porto Alegre, Paulo had practised the guitar four hours a day all summer. On the first day of term, a new student, Sofia, sat down and played a piece so clean and fast that the whole room went quiet. Paulo smiled and clapped with the others. Inside, something dropped. He walked home the long way, past the river, thinking: she's just born with it. I'll never get there. Four hours a day for nothing. When his teacher suggested he and Sofia practise duets, Paulo said he was too busy. He skipped the next ensemble class. That night he didn't pick up his guitar at all. Her playing kept looping in his head, and each time it felt like something was being taken from him.

qa.q: How many hours a day had Paulo practised all summer?
qa.a: Four hours a day.

qa.q: Why did Sofia's playing make Paulo feel something dropped inside?
qa.a: He felt threatened and envious, believing the gap was fixed and that her talent meant his work was for nothing.

qa.q: What could Paulo try instead of avoiding Sofia?
qa.a: He could accept the duet practice and watch how she works, treating her skill as something he can learn from.

qa.q: How might Sofia feel when Paulo avoids the duet?
qa.a: Sofia might feel confused or unwelcome as a new student, not knowing why he pulled away.

grounding: It shows a student who sees a peer excel, decides the gap is destiny, and feels threatened rather than inspired.

passage: The engineering lab in the second-year block smelled of solder. Lakshmi was still wiring her circuit when Jeevan, across the bench, finished his and got it working on the first try. The lab assistant said, loudly, "That's how it's done." Lakshmi felt her chest tighten. Jeevan had topped the last test too. She looked at her tangle of wires and thought, some people just have the brain for this. I don't. Jeevan leaned over. "Want me to show you the trick with the resistor?" "I'm fine," she said, too quickly. She finished late and badly. Back in the hostel, she scrolled through Jeevan's photos, his prizes and certificates, and each one felt like a loss of her own.

qa.q: What did the lab assistant say when Jeevan's circuit worked?
qa.a: "That's how it's done."

qa.q: Why did Lakshmi say 'I'm fine' too quickly when Jeevan offered help?
qa.a: She felt threatened and envious, believing the gap was fixed, so accepting help felt like admitting she could never match him.

qa.q: What could Lakshmi try next time Jeevan offers help?
qa.a: She could accept and treat his trick as something to learn, seeing his skill as a sign that practice pays off.

qa.q: How might Jeevan feel after Lakshmi turns down his offer?
qa.a: Jeevan might feel a little rejected or confused, having meant only to help.

grounding: It shows a student who sees a peer excel, decides the gap is destiny, and feels threatened instead of inspired.

passage:
Dear Jahnavi,

College is fine. I mean, the classes are fine. There's this girl in my literature section, Revati, and I'm trying to explain why she bothers me.

She writes like she's been doing it forever. Her essays get read out every week. The professor quotes her. I used to be the writer at our school, remember? Now I'm just... one of the others.

I know I should be inspired. But every time her name is called, I feel like something is being taken away from me. Like there's only so much talent and she got mine.

I've stopped sharing my drafts in the workshop. What's the point? I'll never write like that.

Tell me I'm being silly.

Vinita

qa.q: Whose essays get read out every week?
qa.a: Revati's essays get read out every week.

qa.q: Why does Vinita feel something is being taken away when Revati's name is called?
qa.a: Vinita feels envious and threatened, as if there's only a fixed amount of talent and Revati's success means a personal loss.

qa.q: What would you advise Vinita?
qa.a: Keep sharing drafts in the workshop and maybe ask Revati how she works, treating her writing as something to learn from rather than a verdict.

qa.q: How might Jahnavi respond to this letter?
qa.a: Jahnavi might feel concerned and eager to remind Vinita of past talent and that writing grows with practice, not a fixed gift.

grounding: It shows a student who sees a peer excel, decides the gap is fixed, and feels threatened rather than inspired.
